text: Then the LORD answered Job:
Will the one who argues with the Almighty accept correction? Let him who accuses God give an answer.
Then Job answered the LORD:
See, I am of little worth—what can I reply to you? I lay my hand over my mouth.
I have spoken once, and I will not answer again; twice, and I will say no more.
Then the LORD answered Job out of the storm:
Brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you will inform me.
Would you really annul my justice? Would you condemn me to justify yourself?
Do you have an arm like God's? Can you thunder with a voice like his?
Then deck yourself with majesty and grandeur; clothe yourself in glory and splendor.

versions.text: Then deck yourself with majesty and height; clothe yourself in glory and splendor.
versions.explanation: "Height" is a wooden rendering of גֹּבַהּ here; in this context it denotes loftiness or exalted grandeur. "Grandeur" preserves the sense and reads far better aloud alongside "majesty."

text: Pour out the fury of your anger; look on every proud man and bring him low.
Look on every proud man and humble him; crush the wicked where they stand.
Bury them in the dust together; shroud their faces in the hidden place.
Then even I would praise you, that your own right hand can save you.

versions.text: Then even I would praise you, for your own right hand had saved you.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew imperfect תוֹשִׁעַ expresses capability in a hypothetical condition, not a completed past act; "had saved" also clashes in tense with "would praise."

text: Look now at Behemoth, which I made along with you; he eats grass like an ox.
Look at the strength in his loins, the power in the muscles of his belly.
He stiffens his tail like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are woven tight.
His bones are tubes of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron.
He is the first of God's works; only his Maker can bring a sword against him.
The mountains yield him their produce, and all the wild animals play there.

versions.text: The hills yield him their produce, and all the wild animals play there.
versions.explanation: הָרִים means "mountains"; "hills" understates the term, and elsewhere the translation keeps such distinctions.

text: He lies down under the lotus trees, hidden among the reeds of the marsh.
The lotus trees cover him with their shade; the willows of the stream surround him.
Though the river rages, he is not alarmed; he is unshaken though the Jordan surges against his mouth.
Can anyone capture him while he watches, or pierce his nose with a snare?
Can you haul in Leviathan with a hook, or tie down his tongue with a rope?
Can you run a cord through his nose, or pierce his jaw with a barb?
Will he plead with you again and again? Will he speak soft words to you?
Will he make a covenant with you, so you can take him as a slave for life?
Will you play with him as with a bird, or leash him for your servant girls?
Will traders haggle over him? Will they divide him among the merchants?
Can you fill his hide with harpoons, or his head with fishing spears?
Lay a hand on him—remember the battle; you will never try again!

versions.text: Lay a hand on him, and you will remember the battle and never try again.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two imperatives ("lay" and "remember") followed by a warning; the current wording flattens the imperative "remember" into a prediction. The revised line keeps the punch and the oral rhythm.
